metrics.title: Technology professionals
metrics.question: How many people with the skills we need are available today?
metrics.note: The national technology workforce, which is what 'available today' means for someone hiring. For context, 2.36M work in India GCCs and 1.4M of those are in technology roles — proof of adoption rather than available supply. A floor, hence atLeast.

metrics.title: Managers and above
metrics.question: Is there a management layer here, or would every lead be an import?
metrics.unit: professionals in manager and above roles
metrics.note: A floor. Sits between bench strength and leadership depth as the middle of the pyramid.

metrics.title: Professionals with 10+ years
metrics.question: Is there a senior layer here we could hire our leadership from?
metrics.note: The size of the experienced layer, not a count of people who have run a specific team size — the narrower claims that used to sit here were not answerable from the supplied data. Separately, 400+ India-based leaders hold global mandates, which is a different claim and has no metric.

metrics.title: Graduate pipeline into technology
metrics.question: Will the talent pool still be deep enough tomorrow, as we grow?
metrics.note: Both figures are GRADUATE_OUTPUT's own parts, unchanged. Deliberately NOT aggregated with computer science and IT (300K) or electronics and communication (250K): those are counted separately in the shared metric and an aggregate engineering total needs ANSR's approval of what counts as engineering. Deliberately NOT nested: 450K is total management and MBA output, not MBA graduates with an engineering background, so no containment and no overlap percentage. The full nine-discipline split is still on the operations and HR tabs.

metrics.title: Talent depth by specialism
metrics.question: Is the depth spread across the specialisms we need, or concentrated in one?
metrics.note: Specialisms overlap, so these do not sum to the bench strength figure. Every part is a floor. Quality engineering was a seeded part with no figure behind it and was removed.

metrics.title: GCCs above 100 tech FTEs
metrics.question: How many centres have already grown past the size we are aiming for?
metrics.note: Roughly 60% of 2,117 centres. About 450 are above 1,000 FTEs, which the metric definition does not cover.

metrics.title: Developers on GitHub
metrics.question: Are engineers here building in the open, or only inside their employers?
metrics.note: Second largest developer population globally, around 13% of global public contributions, with roughly 2.9M new accounts a year. GitLab and Kaggle were seeded parts with no figures and were removed, which makes this a single figure rather than a split.

metrics.title: Capability against other GCC hubs
metrics.question: Where does India lead the alternatives we are also considering, and where is it merely level?
metrics.note: India, Poland and the Philippines are the worked example in docs/brief.md. Vietnam is rated illustratively — the brief names it as a comparator but never rates it, and the supplied comparison was prose about headcount scale rather than capability. Vietnam reads as emerging: competitive on product engineering, thinner on AI and security. Replace with a real assessment before this ships.

metrics.title: Technology professionals
metrics.question: How many people with the skills we need are available today?
metrics.note: The national technology workforce, which is what 'available today' means for someone hiring. For context, 2.36M work in India GCCs and 1.4M of those are in technology roles — proof of adoption rather than available supply. A floor, hence atLeast.

metrics.title: Graduate output by discipline
metrics.question: Will the talent pool still be deep enough tomorrow, as we grow?
metrics.note: Roughly 2.55M STEM graduates a year against roughly 4.5M general graduates. The parts are disjoint. Human resources is postgraduate output from MBA and MSW programmes, which is why it is an order of magnitude below the rest.

metrics.title: Time to backfill a role
metrics.question: When somebody leaves, how long does the seat stay empty?
metrics.note: Mid-level 35–45 days, specialist 60–75. The wider span is stored so neither case is hidden. End labels are deliberately absent: naming them would re-introduce the per-function split this metric exists to collapse.

metrics.title: Time to first hire
metrics.question: How soon could somebody actually start work?
metrics.note: A week on an employer of record, up to ten weeks hiring direct into your own entity. The split that matters is the operating model, which is why the ends are labelled with it — the operations tab used to carry an unlabelled 42–70 instead, which hid the fastest route entirely.

structure.maxLabel: Hiring directly into your own entity

metrics.title: Time to reach each scale milestone
metrics.question: Once the first team proves out, how quickly do centres here add the next hundred?
metrics.note: Months rather than days, as supplied — converting would invent precision. The 100 FTE milestone was given as 9–12 months and the 500 as 500–600 FTEs in 36; the conservative end of each is stored. The HR tab used to omit the 50 FTE step, which made the curve look slower off the line than it is.

metrics.title: Grade A stock, top 7 cities, mn sq ft
metrics.question: Is there space we could move into at the quality our people expect?
metrics.note: Both figures rather than a choice between them: total stock answers whether the market is deep, and vacant answers whether we could move in now. Across the top seven cities at 15.5% vacancy; Bengaluru alone holds 241 msf of the total. `subset` is authored because vacant stock is genuinely part of total stock — the shared unit alone never established that.

entries: Total Grade A stock, top seven cities

metrics.title: Uptime at a Grade A campus
metrics.question: Can we run a shift here without planning around outages?
metrics.note: Split because the campus figure and the grid figure answer different worries, and a single number would hide the weaker one.

entries: At a Grade A campus with N+1 backup

metrics.title: Network latency to cloud regions
metrics.question: Will our teams be working at the same responsiveness as the rest of the business?
metrics.note: Upper end of each supplied range, so nothing reads better than it is: 2–8 ms intra-city to the Mumbai, Hyderabad and Chennai regions, 25–40 ms inter-city. Singapore was a seeded part with no figure and was removed.

metrics.title: Working days lost a year, by city
metrics.question: How many working days a year does the city actually lose?
metrics.note: By city, as supplied, rather than by cause — the seeded split of power, flooding and transit had no figures behind it. Monsoon, civic strikes and extreme weather together account for 3–6 days nationally.

metrics.title: Offer acceptance rate
metrics.question: When we make an offer here, does it get taken?
metrics.note: One national figure. It was a four-city split, which invited a city comparison this screen is not making and cannot support — the visitor has not chosen a city at this point, and picking one for them reads as a recommendation. The supplied city ranges were Bengaluru 62–68, Hyderabad 72–78, Pune 75–82, Chennai 78–85, and offer dropout runs 10–28% depending on the city.

metrics.title: Where salary pressure is strongest
metrics.question: How fast is the cost of the same person rising?
metrics.unit: Base salary growth, year on year
metrics.note: Split by specialism because a single average hides the scarce skills, which is where a plan actually gets repriced. Ordered descending so the ranking states its own axis in row one; 'All roles' carries '(reference)' because it is the comparator the other four are read against, and the label rather than the colour is what says so.

metrics.title: HR support ratio
metrics.question: How many employees does each HR person support once the centre is running, against while it is still being built?
metrics.note: Retitled from 'HR cost per employee served', then shortened from 'HR support ratio per employee served' — the trailing clause duplicated the unit. The supplied cost figure was an absolute annual amount per employee, which this schema cannot hold and the brief forbids showing; the staffing ratio is the part of the brief's own definition that survives. To restore the cost view, supply it as an index against the sending country.

metrics.title: Fully loaded cost by role family and level
metrics.question: How does the all-in cost of a role compare with the same role in the sending country, once statutory contributions, facilities, IT and HR support are counted?
metrics.indexBaseline: Same role in the sending country = 100
metrics.note: Indices only, never amounts — the supplied figures were absolute annual costs per role, which cannot be stored here and which the brief forbids showing in any lens. These cells are illustrative and carry the shape the real data must take: cheapest at the junior end, and the advantage narrowing steadily with seniority, because leadership is the scarce thing everywhere. Loading is roughly 1.35 times base, which is already inside these numbers rather than stated separately.

metrics.title: India wage growth, year on year
metrics.question: Is the cost of the same person here rising faster than we can plan for?
metrics.note: India only. It used to sit beside US and UK wage growth and a 'the advantage narrowing' line, which turned one readable number into a three-way comparison a finance leader has to reconcile — and the narrowing figure was a derived opinion rather than a measurement. The gap is still 55–65% and is held to be durable to around 2032; that belongs in the conversation, not on a bar.

metrics.title: Operating cost growth, year on year
metrics.question: Is the cost of running the centre — utilities, transport, facilities management, local support — rising faster than the wage bill?
metrics.note: PLACEHOLDER at 10% — a demo figure, not a measurement. The operating-cost third of the brief's cost-durability metric; the compensation third is fin-cost-growth at 9.8%. Nothing supplied covers this one: the tier spread is a LEVEL difference between tier 1 and tier 2 rather than a movement over time, and no year-on-year operating figure exists in the supplied data. Deliberately not derived from the wage figure — the two move on different drivers, which is why the brief asks for them separately. Replace with a real rate before publication.

metrics.title: Workplace cost growth, year on year
metrics.question: Is the cost of the space itself rising, and by enough to change a five-year plan?
metrics.note: PLACEHOLDER at 10% — a demo figure, not a measurement. The workplace third of the brief's cost-durability metric. The nearest supplied figures are a 15.5% vacancy rate across the top seven cities and the Bengaluru sub-market rent card behind fin-workplace-cost-gradient — both a position at one moment, neither a rate of change, and a gradient across sub-markets is not a movement over time. Rent growth is the figure to ask for, national or Bengaluru, stated as a percentage. Replace before publication.

metrics.title: What drives the cost advantage
metrics.question: Where does the saving actually come from?
metrics.note: A directional split, and these four sum to a whole.

metrics.title: Tier 1 and tier 2 operating cost spread
metrics.question: What would we save by going beyond the established hubs?
metrics.note: Indices, not amounts. Conservative end of each supplied range: all-in 25–35% below, compensation 15–22% lower, rent roughly half. Attrition also runs 4–6 points lower in tier 2, which is not a cost and has no slot here.

metrics.title: Cost against other GCC hubs
metrics.question: For the same work, how does India sit against the alternatives?
metrics.note: By umbrella function rather than by role. The single 'Senior engineer' row was derived from the one comparison the source supplied, and one engineering row cannot answer the question a finance leader is actually asking — which is what the whole centre costs, function by function. The technology row is that original derivation; the other three carry the same shape and are illustrative until real per-function comparisons are supplied. Separately, India runs about 2.1 heads for every one US head. Vietnam was a seeded column with no figure and was removed.

metrics.title: Cost position against ecosystem depth
metrics.question: Does a cheaper city still carry the talent depth, peer presence, infrastructure and room to scale to execute there?
metrics.note: By city rather than by tier, as supplied. Both rows are indexed on Bengaluru so they can be read against each other, which is the whole point: tier 2 is 30–35% cheaper but thin above 300 FTEs, so cost falls faster than depth. Pune and tier 2 depth are described only qualitatively in the source and are filled illustratively here.

metrics.title: Workplace cost gradient
metrics.question: How much does the workplace cost change as we move out from the centre?
metrics.note: Indexed from the Bengaluru sub-market rent card, so no per-square-foot amount is stored anywhere. The fall from centre to periphery is roughly 60%.
